Expectation1: Help out during difficult times or emergencies.
Situation1: A friend who has just started assembling furniture asks for a quick video call because the instructions are confusing.
Expectation2: Provide emotional support and companionship to patients
Situation2: A patient has just received a difficult diagnosis and is visibly distressed and crying.
Story: I was in the break room, scrolling through my phone during a short lull, when my friend’s message popped up: “Can you hop on a quick video call? I’m losing my mind with this furniture!” I could almost hear the frustration in her text, and I knew she’d just moved in—she didn’t have anyone else nearby. I wanted to be there for her, to laugh about the confusing instructions and help her feel less alone. But just as I was about to reply, I heard a soft sob from down the hall. Mrs. Carter, one of my patients, had just learned her cancer had returned. She was sitting on her bed, shoulders shaking, tears streaming down her face. My heart twisted. As a nursing assistant, I was expected to be her comfort, her steady presence in this moment of fear. I stood frozen, phone in hand, torn between the friend who needed me and the patient who depended on me. The weight of both expectations pressed down, and I felt the sting of not being able to be everything to everyone at once.
